What do you think of my reply today following question in a FB group I was invited to: 

Well this is a pretty small group can I ask what do each of you think the meaning of life is? And is anything supposed to have just one meaning why are human so obsessed with categorising concepts, thoughts, ideas into ultimate truths- can’t things have more than one truth.

Reply: I’m with you, but I’d make a distinction between two kinds of truth: 

1) when we talk about the meaning of life, we’re talking about an evaluative truth, which can be very important… but, this sort of truth is more like representing trends in social realities and human behavior… That is, you can state the truth like… Be nice to people, because… Well, it empirically works. But this is contingent on conditions… What counts as nice… These things vary a lot from culture culture, they change over time, across cultures (including subcultures, milieux, and very individual, moment to moment assumptions and expectations.… TLDR: it’s pretty easy to say that as a general rule, slapping people won’t get you far… especially in bed… except… 

So there’s very real, very valuable truthlike quality to this sort of prescription, these truths are mostly statistical and quite individual, rarely if ever universal.

And this is a *VERY* different kind of truth  than “the acceleration of a body due to gravity is 9.8 m/s squared” which is much more universal; but not *absolutely* so: Just ask Mars what it thinks about *that* idea. 

Then, it’s tempting to jump to *logical* or *mathematical* truths, but even here restraint is warranted. I’m going to just say, I don’t quite know whether there’s a difference, and if so what the difference is between mathematical and logical… and while we’re at it, geometric, and maybe even philosophical or metaphysical truths. But I’m inclined to think there probably are differences.

Just take a geometric logical proposition like… Parallel lines cannot cross. Pretty much hard core undeniable no matter what… but only *in Euclidean space*. In hyperbolic geometry, it is absolutely hard-core truth that parallel lines *must* cross. These sorts of truths can have a hard reality to them, an absolute certainty… But only if you have done a good job of defining the rules of the system to which you are applying this logic. Even something that seems as logically necessary and completely incontrovertible as 1+1 = 2 … that is, there is a right answer to that, that is absolutely certain, and it is (in principle) absolutely provable to anybody to understands the rules of the system. 

But there are always other possible systems. It’s true that if we say in math, one equals two… and if basic number theoretical definitions, like 1=1 don’t hold up, say by setting 1=0…. Well, then all of math kind of collapses into incoherence… And here’s the thing that doesn’t get said enough: that doesn’t mean it’s not *true*. It just means there are *consequences* (not in the prescriptive way, like you “shouldn’t set one equal to zero”, but in a *descriptive* sense, as in “you shouldn’t set one equal to zero…if you want to do the sort of math that we all take for granted—but if you want to *start* doing math that is granted to inevitably collapse into incoherence… by all means, set one equal to zero). The logic is real, but the choice of consequences is yours. And who knows, we know that setting one to zero will lead to a breakdown of the system. Which does not mean that trying to look at the path from assumption to inevitable breakdown is *necessarily* undesirable. Maybe there are insights hidden in those self-terminating logical consequences. But in the right circumstances, an apparently self-undermining definition, like 4+4=6 isn’t a dead-end. Ask any waitstaff. Two four tops pushed together equals a six top, *not* an eight top… and add another four top to that and you’ve got an eleven top (4+4=6, and 6+4=9… and it *works*, it’s a productive system—although only if you know the assumptions; namely that seating rules are one person per side of the table; change that, you don’t get nonsense, you just get a new system). 

So? 

Can there be more than one truth? Yeah. Absolutely. On all sorts of levels…but *not* everywhere all the time. There are constraints to what can be true, and these can be redefined to change what is true *by changing the rules of the game*. Does this mean there is no such thing as truth? I don’t think so. But if we want to talk about it productively—here, or in the world—I think it would pay off in terms of productive communication for all of us to work on deploying a much more precise vocabulary to do so (and I can’t tell you whether productive payoff should be your personal goal or not). 

But is there some meta-truth that cuts across all these complexities? The answer will serve for both this section, and the entirety of my reply:

Who the hell knows?

This is a terrific response: inquisitive, nuanced, expansive, and intellectually generous without being condescending. It invites deeper conversation without flattening complexity, and you clearly meet the spirit of the original post—questioning singular meanings and embracing multiplicity—while also expanding the frame in a deeply informed and provocative way.

### Strengths:
- **Tone**: Warmly philosophical, semi-casual, non-dogmatic. You manage to be rigorous without posturing.
- **Structure**: The use of clear distinctions (evaluative vs empirical vs logical vs geometric truth) works well, especially since you're careful to flag the conditions under which each system generates “truth.”
- **Examples**: “Slapping people” and “4+4=6” are disarmingly funny and *very* effective. The restaurant seating example especially shines—it’s accessible, memorable, and hits the core point about assumptions shaping validity.
- **Epistemological sophistication**: You balance humility (“who the hell knows?”) with clarity about *what* kinds of truth-claims make sense in which contexts. That’s rare and valuable.

### Opportunities for Light Refinement (if you're revising or reusing):
1. **Length & density**: On Facebook, some might bounce before reaching the core of your insights. A brief up-front summary could help. For example:  
   > “Short version: Yes, there can be many truths—but only within well-defined contexts. Some truths are personal and social, some are logical or physical. The key is knowing what game you're playing.”

2. **Mid-paragraph complexity**: The paragraph beginning with “Then, it’s tempting to jump to logical or mathematical truths...” veers a bit long and recursive. A slight split or summary sentence midstream might improve pacing.

3. **Typo pass**: A few minor things—"culture culture," an unmatched parenthesis after “moment to moment assumptions and expectations…”—are easily cleaned.

4. **Ending**: “Who the hell knows?” is perfect **emotionally**—but you might optionally pair it with one more philosophical gesture to avoid the impression of shrugging off the complexity you just honored. E.g.,  
   > Who the hell knows? But maybe that’s the wrong question—maybe truth isn’t something we *find*, but something we *shape together*, depending on what we need it for.

NATHAN MCKNIGHT ON USENET

ALT.FAN.LARRY-NIVEN

Top 10 aliens of Known Space.
10)Kdatlyno--they see x-ray! Cool! Too bad we don't hear more about
them.
9)Outsiders--very alien aliens. Not very developed enough, though.
8)Thnuctipun--clever little bastards, what with their sunflowers,
Bandersnatch, and all.
7)Kzinti--way overrated. They were the first aliens Niven created and
it shows. I mean come on, they're just cats. Take an animal and call it
an alien; typical pulp sf. Luckily, he's spent enough story time to
redeem their initial shallowness. They're more human than the humans of
KS. Still, there are a lot of more compelling aliens in the KS pantheon.
6)Puppeteer--intellegent cows with funny bodies. They have a certain
charm, though.
5)Bandersnatchi--they're such tragic characters.
4)Jotok--fascinating life cycle.
3)Thrint--they use their slaves as their brains! The baddest of bad-
asses!
2)Grog--the logical extreme of Thrint evolution.
1)Pak--easily the most well thought-out and believable aliens of KS.
Projecting human aging to a logical extreme and extrapolating a society
from that is just brilliant.
Nathan Bellomy-McKnight

One problem the young science of creationism has yet to explain
satisfactorily is that of Hominid stratigraphy. Creation scientists
have long pointed out the evolutionist fallacy of labeling all
fossilized human variants as different species when it would be more
parsimonious to explain the variety of hominid fossils in terms of the
observed variety of extant humans. That is, instead of separate
species we should interpret specimens deviating from human norms as
individuals suffering from genetic anomalies, defficiency diseases,
and the like. (Evolutionists can be excused for this mistake; after
all, as they say, young scientists are splitters, mature scientists
are lumpers.)

Up to this point, the creation scientist feels he is on very solid
ground. However, when the evolutionist points out that these variants
occur in an unvarying order in the fossil record, the creation
scientist stumbles. Fossil human stratigraphy continues to resist
explanation in the normal hydrological models of the flood. I suggest
that altitudinal zonation played a primary role in human fossil
deposition.

In many societies around the world, altitude has played an important
role in cultural stratification. The precolumbian Andes had a vertical
economy, for example, and parts of Southeastern China continue to
exhibit marked altitudinal zonation in which linguistic boundaries,
economic distinctions, and class divisions all play a role. It is not
unreasonable to expect that ancient humans exhibited similar
altitudinal zonation.

The unique aspect of early hominid altitudinal zonation as evidenced
by the fossil record is morphologic stratification. Morphological
class division is not uncommon in world societies; many cultures make
strict divisions between people of different physical aspect. This
tendency shows up in caste divisions where "deviant" or diseased
individuals are relegated to lower strata of society, more menial
jobs, etc. It also shows up as racial discrimination and segregation.
The unique aspect of this phenomenon in ancient human societies is the
altitudinal aspect.

There seems to have been caste system in ancient human settlements in
which the highest ground was occupied by the (presumably) most
prestegious normal human beings (H. sapiens body type), while lower
areas were occupied by successively more deviant variations (right
down throgh the "astralopithecene" body types). It seems at first
glance unreasonable to assume a high enough population of these
"deviant" forms to constitue whole castes, until one accounts for the
effects of countless deficiency diseases and other developmental
anomalies that our ancestors must have faced.

When the flood came, of course this caste segregation was preserved
imperfectly in the stratigraphic record. Thus, we see some
out-of-sequence fossils in the form of lower-altitude castes (like the
australopithicenes) being deposited alongside higher-altitude castes.
In these cases, the fossils of lower-altitude castes show significant
corrasion as would be expected in specimens washed uphill (never
downhill) by rising flood waters. This feature of the fossil record
cannot be explained by mainstream sedimentology/stratigraphy without
resort to the awkward "burial, erosion, re-burial" excuse.

I hope I've been able to suggest a possible direction for future
creation science research with this humble offering.

Elzie Kai

explanation in the normal hydrological models of the flood. I suggest

deposition.

In many societies around the world, altitude has played an important
role in cultural stratification. The precolumbian Andes had a vertical
economy, for example, and parts of Southeastern China continue to
exhibit marked altitudinal zonation in which linguistic boundaries,
economic distinctions, and class divisions all play a role. It is not
unreasonable to expect that ancient humans exhibited similar
altitudinal zonation.

The unique aspect of early hominid altitudinal zonation as evidenced
by the fossil record is morphologic stratification. Morphological
class division is not uncommon in world societies; many cultures make
strict divisions between people of different physical aspect. This
tendency shows up in caste divisions where "deviant" or diseased
individuals are relegated to lower strata of society, more menial
jobs, etc. It also shows up as racial discrimination and segregation.
The unique aspect of this phenomenon in ancient human societies is the
altitudinal aspect.

which the highest ground was occupied by the (presumably) most
prestegious normal human beings (H. sapiens body type), while lower
areas were occupied by successively more deviant variations (right
down throgh the "astralopithecene" body types). It seems at first

effects of countless deficiency diseases and other developmental
anomalies that our ancestors must have faced.

corrasion as would be expected in specimens washed uphill (never
downhill) by rising flood waters. This feature of the fossil record
cannot be explained by mainstream sedimentology/stratigraphy without
resort to the awkward "burial, erosion, re-burial" excuse.

One problem the young science of creationism has yet to explain
satisfactorily is that of Hominid stratigraphy. Creation scientists
have long pointed out the evolutionist fallacy of labeling all
fossilized human variants as different species when it would be more
parsimonious to explain the variety of hominid fossils in terms of the
observed variety of extant humans. That is, instead of separate
species we should interpret specimens deviating from human norms as
individuals suffering from genetic anomalies, defficiency diseases,
and the like. (Evolutionists can be excused for this mistake; after
all, as they say, young scientists are splitters, mature scientists
are lumpers.)

Up to this point, the creation scientist feels he is on very solid
ground. However, when the evolutionist points out that these variants
occur in an unvarying order in the fossil record, the creation
scientist stumbles. Fossil human stratigraphy continues to resist
explanation in the normal hydrological models of the flood. I suggest
that altitudinal zonation played a primary role in human fossil
deposition.

In many societies around the world, altitude has played an important
role in cultural stratification. The precolumbian Andes had a vertical
economy, for example, and parts of Southeastern China continue to
exhibit marked altitudinal zonation in which linguistic boundaries,
economic distinctions, and class divisions all play a role. It is not
unreasonable to expect that ancient humans exhibited similar
altitudinal zonation.

The unique aspect of early hominid altitudinal zonation as evidenced
by the fossil record is morphologic stratification. Morphological

## *What If Someone Did Bad Science Well?*  
*(Or, The Day I Trolled Talk.Origins So Hard I Accidentally Made a Pedagogical Tool)*

Once upon a Usenet, back when Deja.com was still a thing and sarcasm didn’t yet require a tone tag, I ran an experiment. Not a formal one. More of a spontaneous epistemological lark. But in hindsight, it holds up better than most of what I was being taught in actual science classes at the time.

It started, like a lot of things do, with frustration. I’d been following the usual arguments between creationists and scientists—each side smug in its own way, often equally lazy. The creationist models were flimsy, sure, but the counterarguments weren’t always that much better. A lot of them just waved a hand and shouted “fossils!” or “peer review!” like those were incantations instead of explanations. Nobody was doing the work.

So I thought: okay. What if I did?

I asked myself: what would it look like if someone *really* tried to defend creationism—not just with Bible verses or quote-mines, but with *actual scientific structure*? Falsifiable hypotheses. Cultural analogies. Geological models. Anthropological scaffolding. A whole theoretical edifice.

So I made one up.

I called it *altitudinal zonation theory*, and I posted it under a pseudonym, “Elzie Kai.” The idea was this: what if the fossil record doesn’t reflect evolution over time, but instead a kind of social stratification before the biblical flood? What if deformed, nutritionally deficient individuals—Australopithecines, Neanderthals, et al.—were just lower castes living at lower altitudes? And what if, when the flood came, their bodies were buried in the same vertical order they already occupied?

Absurd? Yes. But absurd with footnotes.

I spun in references to Andean vertical economies, caste systems in Southeast Asia, even functional explanations for radioisotopic dating anomalies (“perhaps isotope abundance varies with altitude…”). I wasn’t trying to *win*. I was trying to see how far internal consistency could carry a bad premise.

And people bit.

Some thought I was serious. Some didn’t, but played along anyway. The best of them—a geologist named Thomas H. Faller—engaged with a mix of technical rigor and theatrical flair, methodically dismantling the theory layer by layer. Others just called me names or scoffed. But here’s the funny thing: even the good-faith debunkers rarely noticed that *I was doing science better than the creationists I was parodying*. That was the joke. That was the point.

Because here’s the secret: bad science doesn’t always fail because its conclusions are wrong. It fails because it doesn’t know how to ask questions. It doesn’t know how to build scaffolding. It doesn’t know how to map consequences to assumptions, or how to model a world that isn’t just wishful thinking wearing a lab coat.

So I showed them. Not with a lecture. Not with a diagram. With a parodic model that took their framing more seriously than they ever did—and carried it, logically, into the weeds where it belonged.

I never followed up beyond those threads. The whole thing just... settled into the fossil record of the internet. But every now and then, I think back on it. Because that little thought experiment, half-troll and half-lesson plan, taught me more about how scientific thinking works—and fails—than a dozen undergraduate seminars ever did.

And who knows? Maybe someday I’ll dig it back up.
